intro: Read the deck for the rules and these notes for the judgement behind them. Each note under a slide says what to remember, how to apply it in the field and where people slip. Work the exercises in pencil, check yourself with the recall questions, and write your own notes in the space around mine.

sections.title: Why Research Ethics Matters
sections.big_idea: Every row in your data is a person, and ethics is **taking responsibly** from people who often have less power than you.
in_plain_words: Development research takes time, accounts of hard events, identifying details and photographs from people. Each has a cost to them. Research ethics governs how we treat people, communities and data: respect, minimal harm and a fair share of benefits and burdens. It runs from the research question to how findings are used.

Power is unequal, so 'they agreed' is not enough. Most ethical harm comes from convenience, pressure, distance, habit and optimism, and little from malice. Failure damages people, truth, trust and your organisation. **Ethics and data quality rise together**, because coerced answers are unreliable answers.

left.title: Ethics is
items: Applied in the field, under pressure

right.title: Ethics is not
items: A record of having no problems

diagram.caption: the working definition from the deck

key_terms.meaning: Principles governing how we treat people, communities and data in research.
Unequal institutional, linguistic and economic standing between researcher and participant.
Participants shape what is asked, see findings, withdraw and keep a stake.
Studying the poor because they are easy to reach and rarely complain.
Research that takes data and returns nothing.

worked_example.title: Cost the transaction
worked_example.setup: A team interviews a woman for an hour about a difficult event and photographs her at her door.
steps: The hour costs her an hour of earning, cooking or rest.
Retelling the event costs her distress.
Identifying details create exposure risk she cannot control.
The photograph shows how she appears to strangers, indefinitely.
worked_example.answer: Four costs, each borne by her, so each needs a benefit and her informed agreement to justify it.

mistakes: Treating ethics as a signed form and not as continuous judgement.
Assuming good intentions are a safeguard.
Letting an association with a benefit make refusal feel costly without saying so.
Making ethics everyone's job, which makes it nobody's.

recall.q: How does the deck define research ethics?
recall.a: The principles and procedures governing how we treat people, communities and data: respect, minimising harm, and distributing benefits and burdens fairly.

recall.q: Name two reasons ethics fails in practice.
recall.a: Convenience, deadline pressure, distance, habit or optimism.

recall.q: What three things does failure damage besides your organisation?
recall.a: People, truth and trust.

recall.q: What is the test for participant as author?
recall.a: Could you explain your study candidly and in full to the people in it, and would they still agree?

recall.q: What habit makes the next decision better?
recall.a: Writing down the dilemmas you face and how you resolved them.

sections.title: History & Codes
sections.big_idea: Each major code answered a documented abuse, and **the codes lag practice**, which is why you must reason as well as comply.
in_plain_words: Nuremberg (1947) made voluntary consent essential. Helsinki (1964) put the participant's wellbeing ahead of science and, from 1975, introduced independent review. Tuskegee ran from 1932 to 1972 and forced the modern oversight system into being. Belmont (1979) distilled three principles and paired each with a procedure.

CIOMS, ICMR 2017 and the DPDP Act 2023 adapt the principles to low-resource and Indian conditions, where written consent may be meaningless, households decide and refusal carries a perceived cost. **The profession has reformed after exposure and not after reflection.**

key_terms.meaning: 1947 statement that research on humans requires voluntary consent.
World Medical Association guidance; independent review from 1975.
US study (1932-1972) that left syphilis untreated and uninformed.
1979 report with three principles.
Guidelines for low-resource and global settings.

worked_example.title: How long between events?
worked_example.setup: Use the dates on the timeline slide.
steps: Tuskegee ran 1972 − 1932 = 40 years.
Nuremberg to Belmont: 1979 − 1947 = 32 years.
Helsinki (1964) to its independent review revision (1975): 1975 − 1964 = 11 years.
ICMR 2017 to the DPDP Act 2023: 2023 − 2017 = 6 years.

mistakes: Treating the codes as abstract philosophy and not as responses to specific abuses.
Assuming the codes cover data-driven research, which they did not anticipate.
Applying imported assumptions about written consent and individual autonomy unchanged.
Reading Tuskegee as a foreign problem and not as a warning aimed at development research.

recall.q: Which code first said research on humans requires consent?
recall.a: The Nuremberg Code, 1947.

recall.q: What did Helsinki's 1975 revision introduce?
recall.a: Independent ethics review.

recall.q: Why did Tuskegee end?
recall.a: A journalist published it.

recall.q: Which Belmont principle maps to fair selection of participants?
recall.a: Justice.

recall.q: Name two assumptions of imported codes that fail in South Asia.
recall.a: Written consent is meaningful, individual autonomy decides, refusal carries no cost, or a regulator can be reached.

sections.title: Core Principles
sections.big_idea: Respect for persons, beneficence and justice are **weighed against one another**, and newer principles add communities.
in_plain_words: Respect for persons honours competent choices and protects those with reduced autonomy. Beneficence is an active duty to do good, with non-maleficence preventing harm. Justice asks who carries the cost and who collects the benefit. In South Asia the same marginalised communities are surveyed again and again with no feedback.

The principles collide: confidentiality against preventing harm, autonomy against safety, access against voluntariness. Beyond Belmont, add respect for communities, reciprocity, transparency and cultural humility. **Ask all five anchor questions before fieldwork and again before publication.**

children.label: Justice
items: Fair sharing of burden and gain

key_terms.meaning: A competent person's right to decide freely about taking part.
First, do no harm.
Fair sharing of research burdens and benefits.
Giving something back to participants.
Letting local norms shape what consent and respect mean.
Harm to a community from a finding attached to it.

worked_example.title: Apply the principles to a repeat survey
worked_example.setup: A team plans its fifth survey of the same slum near its office, publishing in a foreign journal and returning no results.
steps: Justice: the burden falls on a convenient population, and the benefit flows elsewhere.
Beneficence: the third question fails, because benefits do not reach the risk-bearers.
Respect for persons: ask whether people were told this and chose freely.
Beyond Belmont: reciprocity fails, since nothing is returned. Check whether the question is already answered.
worked_example.answer: The survey fails justice, beneficence and reciprocity, so redesign or reuse existing data.

mistakes: Reading 'protect those with reduced autonomy' as permission to decide for them.
Selecting participants because they are reachable.
Resolving conflicts by default in favour of the principle the deadline serves.
Relying on individual consent when harm falls on a group.

recall.q: What are the Belmont principles?
recall.a: Respect for persons, beneficence and justice.

recall.q: What two halves does respect for persons have?
recall.a: Honour the choices of the autonomous, and protect those with reduced autonomy.

recall.q: What injustice does the deck describe?
recall.a: Study the slum, publish in a foreign journal, change nothing in the slum.

recall.q: Name two newer principles.
recall.a: Respect for communities, reciprocity, transparency or cultural humility.

recall.q: What is the last of the five anchor questions in the table?
recall.a: Could this harm a group?

sections.title: Informed Consent
sections.big_idea: Consent is a **process that continues through the study** and needs voluntariness, disclosure and a comprehension check that someone has made.
in_plain_words: Consent requires understanding, voluntariness, disclosure and the right to stop. Tell participants who you are and who funds the work, what participation involves, risks, how data is used and for how long, the right to refuse, and whom to contact. Funder disclosure and onward sharing are the omissions that matter most.

Where reading is not assumed, explain verbally, use an impartial witness and check comprehension. Pressure from officials, benefits or gatekeepers makes a 'yes' unfree. Children give assent as well as parental permission. Consent can be withdrawn. **Test comprehension and offer refusal actively**, because silence is not agreement.

key_terms.meaning: Voluntary agreement given after understanding what is involved.
A child's own agreement alongside a parent's consent.
A literate witness independent of the pressure being checked for.
Asking the participant to say back what the study is about.
Fresh consent as a long study changes.
A person who controls access to a community.

worked_example.title: A refusal rate as a warning
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a team approaches 200 people in a poor community, and 2 refuse.
steps: Refusal rate: 2 ÷ 200 = 1%.
The deck says a rate near zero is a warning about the process.
Retrain: state the separation from benefits, interview without officials and offer refusal twice.
Offering refusal actively raises refusal rates, which is evidence it had been suppressed.
worked_example.answer: A 1% refusal rate suggests refusal was suppressed, so redesign the consent process.

mistakes: Counting a signature or thumbprint on an unexplained form as consent.
Using a gatekeeper or relative as the impartial witness.
Treating consent for one study as consent for a repository.
Keeping data in a form from which one person's data cannot be found and deleted.

recall.q: What are the three elements of consent?
recall.a: Voluntary, informed and comprehended.

recall.q: What does the deck say about a thumbprint on a form nobody explained?
recall.a: It is not consent; it documents a ritual.

recall.q: When should a child's refusal be respected?
recall.a: Even if a parent agrees; assent works as a veto.

recall.q: What should you do about officials who accompany you?
recall.a: Interview without them.

recall.q: What do you do when a participant is in acute distress?
recall.a: Defer or seek a surrogate, and return when they are stable, or not at all.

sections.title: Vulnerable Populations & Power Asymmetry
sections.big_idea: Vulnerability comes from the situation, so the answer is **extra safeguards for the group inside the study**.
in_plain_words: A vulnerable population has constrained capacity to give free consent or protect its interests, through poverty, age, dependence, stigma or lack of power. It is a feature of the situation and says nothing about the person's weakness. Groups include people in poverty, children, women in some settings, Dalit and Adivasi people, persons with disability and refugees.

Poverty turns inducement into pressure, so compensate for time and cost only. Gender needs private interviews and trained women interviewers. Caste research can cause group harm. For refugees the safest data is the data you did not collect. **Leaving groups out designs programmes for them on evidence that does not include them.**

key_terms.meaning: A group whose capacity to consent or protect its interests is constrained.
A payment or promise large enough to override free choice.
Communities studied repeatedly with no return.
Declining cooperation and cynicism from repeated surveys.
A known route to send someone who is distressed or in danger.

worked_example.title: Is the payment proportionate?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: local daily earnings are Rs 400 over an 8-hour day, and an interview takes 1.5 hours.
steps: Hourly value of time: 400 ÷ 8 = 50 rupees.
Time value of the interview: 50 × 1.5 = 75 rupees.
A payment near Rs 75 compensates time and is fair.
A payment of Rs 500 is 500 − 400 = 100 rupees above a full day's earnings, so consent is compromised.
worked_example.answer: About Rs 75 is proportionate; Rs 500 would compromise consent.

mistakes: Treating vulnerability as a label on people and excluding them.
Payment announced publicly or tied to a benefit.
Repeating a woman's answers to her family, even approvingly.
Asking about violence or illness with no referral route ready.

recall.q: What does vulnerability come from?
recall.a: Dependence on the researcher or a benefit, restricted ability to refuse, stigma and legal or physical exposure.

recall.q: What should compensation be for?
recall.a: Time and cost; a payment for taking part itself is an inducement.

recall.q: What does the deck advise for refugees' data?
recall.a: Collect the minimum identifying data, or none.

recall.q: What safeguard is most often missing?
recall.a: Referral.

recall.q: What does over-researching show as?
recall.a: Declining cooperation and open cynicism.

sections.title: Privacy, Confidentiality & Anonymity
sections.big_idea: Privacy, confidentiality and anonymity are three distinct duties, and **deleting names is only the beginning of anonymisation**.
in_plain_words: Privacy belongs to the participant and is violated in the room. Confidentiality is your duty to protect what they entrusted, and it breaks most often through a remark between enumerators. Anonymity is a property of the data, and quasi-identifiers such as village, age, caste and occupation can re-identify a person in a small area.

Risk rises as the area shrinks. Secure the data with encryption, unique passwords, a separate name-code key and deletion dates, and remember paper. Sensitive categories raise the bar, and honest limits beat blanket promises. **Publish at the smallest unit your analysis needs and no smaller.**

diagram.caption: how a de-identified file gives someone away

key_terms.meaning: The person's right to control access to themselves and their information.
Your duty to protect the data entrusted to you.
Data that cannot be traced back to the individual.
A trait that identifies a person in combination.
Use age bands or districts instead of exact values.
The link between names and responses, stored separately.

worked_example.title: How many cells are there?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a village file has 1,000 people, 10 age bands, 4 castes and 5 occupations.
steps: Combinations of the three variables: 10 × 4 × 5 = 200.
Average records per combination: 1,000 ÷ 200 = 5.
People are not spread evenly, so some combinations will hold just one or two records.
Those cells identify a household, so coarsen or remove them before sharing.
worked_example.answer: 200 combinations, an average of 5 per cell, but the smallest cells are the risk.

mistakes: Promising anonymity because names were deleted.
Storing the name-code key in the same folder as the data.
Leaving completed consent forms in an unlocked field office.
Promising 'completely confidential' when a court order or small sample can defeat it.

recall.q: Who does privacy belong to?
recall.a: The participant.

recall.q: How can anonymity fail without any names?
recall.a: Quasi-identifiers combine to match one person in a small area.

recall.q: What remedies does the deck list?
recall.a: Aggregate geography, band ages and suppress rare categories.

recall.q: What should you say instead of 'This is completely confidential'?
recall.a: 'We will protect this, and here are the limits.'

recall.q: What is the most-forgotten security risk?
recall.a: Paper forms.

sections.title: Do No Harm & Risk–Benefit Assessment
sections.big_idea: Social research harms in invisible ways, so **estimate likelihood and severity** for five kinds of harm and keep the stop option real.
in_plain_words: Development research rarely involves needles, so it is wrongly assumed harmless. Five harms matter: physical, psychological, social, legal and economic. The most damaging are often invisible, occurring after you leave. A follow-up conversation weeks later is the practical way to find out whether harm occurred.

Risk is likelihood times severity. High-high should be redesigned, and low-high needs a prepared response. Minimal risk must be judged through the participant's eyes. The five-step risk-benefit sequence ends with redesign or stop. Protect your staff from secondary trauma, and **design harm out**: drop the high-risk, low-value question.

diagram.note: high x high: redesign; low x high: mitigate and prepare; low x low: proceed

key_terms.meaning: Anticipate and prevent injury of every kind.
Weighing identified harms against benefits.
Risk no greater than daily life or routine interviews.
Distress suffered by field staff who hear accounts of violence.
A design change that lowers risk, such as dropping a question.

worked_example.title: Score three questions
worked_example.setup: Illustrative scale: likelihood and severity each from 1 (low) to 3 (high).
steps: A question on legal status: likelihood 2, severity 3, so 2 × 3 = 6.
A question on the favourite meal: 1 × 1 = 1.
A probing question to a survivor: likelihood 3, severity 3, so 3 × 3 = 9.
Act by the matrix: 9 is high-high, so redesign; 6 sits in the middle and needs mitigation and ethics review; 1 can proceed.
worked_example.answer: Scores of 6, 1 and 9: mitigate the legal question, proceed with the meal question, redesign the survivor question.

mistakes: Treating 'it's only a survey' as a safe default.
Using 'we saw no problems' as evidence of no harm.
Discounting rare catastrophic outcomes.
Making proceed the only possible outcome of a risk-benefit analysis.

recall.q: What are the five kinds of harm?
recall.a: Physical, psychological, social, legal and economic.

recall.q: What does the matrix prescribe for high likelihood and high severity?
recall.a: Redesign; do not proceed as planned.

recall.q: What is the minimal-risk benchmark?
recall.a: Risk no greater than ordinarily encountered in daily life or routine interviews and examinations.

recall.q: What is the cheapest, most common mitigation?
recall.a: Dropping a single high-risk, low-value question.

recall.q: Why is secondary trauma also a data issue?
recall.a: Distressed enumerators collect worse data and make worse judgements.

sections.title: Ethics Review in India
sections.big_idea: Independent review exists because researchers cannot judge their own ethics, and in India **ICMR 2017** is the benchmark.
in_plain_words: A body with no stake in the result checks that participants are protected before data collection. An Institutional Ethics Committee is India's counterpart of the IRB, with independent, lay, legal and gender-balanced members. ICMR 2017 sets the principal framework, covering social and behavioural research in health as well as clinical work.

Clinical trials of drugs and devices fall under the DCGI and CDSCO. A committee asks about value and design, consent, risk-benefit, vulnerable groups, privacy and justice. **Submit before any data collection**, with local-language consent materials, and report adverse events promptly. Retrospective approval is not approval.

key_terms.meaning: Institutional Ethics Committee, the Indian counterpart of the IRB.
National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research.
Drugs Controller General of India, under CDSCO.
The first ICMR principle: is the research needed at all?
Approval sought after data collection, which does not cure it.

worked_example.title: Which route for each study?
steps: A household survey on nutrition and wellbeing falls within ICMR 2017's social and behavioural scope, so go to an IEC.
A trial of a drug or device falls under DCGI and CDSCO, with a registered committee.
A study whose organisation has no committee uses an external or shared IEC.
In all three, submit before collecting anything.
worked_example.answer: IEC, DCGI-regulated trial approval, and an external IEC respectively.

mistakes: Assuming social research needs no review because nobody requires it.
Submitting English consent forms for a local-language study.
Treating reviewers' questions as obstruction.
Seeking approval after data collection.

recall.q: Which members should a good IEC include?
recall.a: Scientists, a clinician, a legal expert, an ethicist and a lay member representing the community.

recall.q: Which version did ICMR 2017 update?
recall.a: ICMR's 2006 version.

recall.q: What are the four ICMR emphases?
recall.a: Essentiality and voluntariness, non-exploitation, privacy and confidentiality, accountability and transparency.

recall.q: Who regulates clinical trials in India?
recall.a: The Drugs Controller General of India under CDSCO.

recall.q: What does skipping review risk?
recall.a: Voiding publication, breaching funder rules and leaving participants unprotected.

sections.title: Field Realities & Dilemmas
sections.big_idea: Textbook ethics meets crowds, gatekeepers and tears, so **decide the rule in advance** and protect the person with least power.
in_plain_words: Gatekeepers give access and local legitimacy but not consent, and their presence can make honest answers impossible. Incentives sharpen in the field: a crowd gathers, people answer to qualify, gatekeepers expect a share. Pay directly and privately, after the interview.

When a participant discloses serious harm, confidentiality collides with a duty to prevent harm, so state the limits first and know your legal duties, including POCSO. Photographs are identifiable data and need separate consent. The family test guards dignity. **Use the five-step method** and document your reasoning.

diagram.caption: a method for the dilemma in front of you

key_terms.meaning: A person controlling access to a community, such as a sarpanch or employer.
An obligation to act when you learn of serious harm.
A legal duty to report, for example under POCSO.
Would I accept this image of my own family?
Images that strip dignity from people.

worked_example.title: A disclosure in the doorway
worked_example.setup: A participant says a child in her house is being abused, and your consent form did not mention reporting.
steps: Name the conflict: confidentiality against preventing harm.
Ask who is affected: the child most, and the participant too.
Options: report under your legal duty, tell the participant first, and use your referral route.
Decide for the most vulnerable person, document it, and revise the consent script to state the limit up front.
worked_example.answer: Protect the child, follow the reporting duty, document, and fix the consent script.

mistakes: Accepting a gatekeeper's permission as the participant's consent.
Announcing payment publicly.
Warning a participant about reporting only after they disclose.
Reading a field team's distress as an attitude problem.

recall.q: What does gatekeeper permission not give you?
recall.a: Any individual's consent, freedom from their influence, a representative sample or voluntariness.

recall.q: What should you do before fieldwork about disclosure?
recall.a: Decide what triggers it, to whom you would report, what you tell the participant and who decides.

recall.q: What is the family test?
recall.a: Would I be comfortable if this were a photo of my own family, captioned this way, seen by my neighbours and employer?

recall.q: What is the tie-breaker rule?
recall.a: Where principles conflict irreducibly, protect the person with least power.

recall.q: Which signs show secondary traumatic stress in a team?
recall.a: Emotional flatness, avoiding interviews, sleep and appetite changes, cynicism about participants.

sections.title: Data Ethics, Ownership & Dissemination
sections.big_idea: Ethics continues after the field: **who owns, shares and reports the data** matters as much as consent.
in_plain_words: Storage, analysis, ownership, sharing and reporting are decisions made months after consent by people who never met a participant. Communities are often extracted from, so ask who owns and profits, leave a usable copy behind and return findings in a form people can use, with a budget line and a date.

The DPDP Act 2023 applies from 13 May 2027, and its research exemption is narrow. FAIR optimises data for use, and CARE asks who benefits and who decides. Releasing micro-data on marginalised people can enable re-identification. **Report accurately**: no over-claiming, no cherry-picking, no stripping of dignity.

right.title: CARE
items: Risk alone: data that helps nobody

key_terms.meaning: Whose data it is and who profits from it.
Returning findings and value to those studied.
India's data-protection law, with duties from 13 May 2027.
A narrow research exemption with conditions.
A data-use agreement and approved-researcher route.

worked_example.title: Check a file before release
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a micro-data file has 120 combinations of quasi-identifiers, and 14 of them match only one or two records.
steps: Share of risky cells: 14 ÷ 120 = 11.7%.
Each such cell could identify a household.
Coarsen the variables or suppress those cells.
Check whether consent covered sharing; if not, do not release, or use controlled access.
worked_example.answer: About 11.7% of cells are risky, so coarsen or suppress them and confirm consent before release.

mistakes: Assuming open data is automatically ethical.
Promising to share results 'later' with no budget or date.
Letting a funder veto findings after they exist.
Assuming a small NGO is exempt from the DPDP Act.

recall.q: When do the DPDP duties and the 17(2)(b) exemption apply?
recall.a: From 13 May 2027.

recall.q: What does CARE stand for?
recall.a: Collective benefit, Authority to control, Responsibility, Ethics.

recall.q: What is the clearest practical form of reciprocity?
recall.a: Leaving a usable copy of the data and the findings with the community.

recall.q: When is 17(2)(b) available?
recall.a: When no decision specific to an individual is taken and the Second Schedule standards are followed.

recall.q: What should you agree before the work starts?
recall.a: Publication rights.

sections.title: Putting It to Work
sections.big_idea: Three checklists and a set of red flags turn principles into **habits for each stage** of a study.
in_plain_words: The planning checklist asks whether the research is necessary, who bears the risk and who gains, whether a committee has reviewed it, whether consent forms are in the local language and whether vulnerable participants have extra safeguards. The cheapest improvement is checking whether existing data answers your question.

The fieldwork checklist applies every day, because consent quality degrades under quota pressure. The data checklist covers secure storage, re-identification, DPDP duties, returning findings and deleting identifiers. Five sentences are red flags. **Spot-check interviews yourself** and put the deletion date in a calendar with an owner.

key_terms.meaning: Five questions answered in writing before fieldwork.
Daily checks on consent, refusal, privacy, referral and team support.
A routine sentence that signals harm ahead.
Observing interviews unannounced.
A date written into the protocol for removing identifiers.

worked_example.title: Plan a spot-check
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a team of enumerators will complete 40 interviews in a village cluster, and you will spot-check 10% unannounced.
steps: Interviews to observe: 40 × 10 ÷ 100 = 4.
Watch for speed and missing comprehension checks.
Listen for implied benefits, a crowd or a gatekeeper.
Check whether limits of confidentiality were stated, and give feedback the same day.
worked_example.answer: Observe 4 interviews, looking for the failure signs in the fieldwork checklist.

mistakes: Surveying again without checking whether existing data answers the question.
Treating a red-flag sentence as a reasonable remark.
Checking consent once at the start of fieldwork.
Setting no deletion date, so risk has no end.

recall.q: How many planning questions does the checklist have?
recall.a: Five.

recall.q: Why is the 'incentive is large' flag counter-intuitive?
recall.a: Universal agreement in a poor community is evidence about the inducement and says nothing about the study.

recall.q: How often should the fieldwork checks be done?
recall.a: Every day through fieldwork, since consent quality degrades under quota pressure.

recall.q: Which source is short enough to read in an hour?
recall.a: The Belmont Report.

recall.q: What is the takeaway to adopt if you take only one?
recall.a: Consent is a process: voluntary, informed, understood, revocable.

notes.2: Read the agenda as a path from reasons to rules to practice. Sections 1 to 3 give you the history and the three principles, sections 4 to 7 apply them to consent, vulnerability, privacy and harm, and sections 8 to 11 cover review, the field, data and checklists. If you are short of time, start with section 4.
notes.4: Begin with the transaction table. Every hour, story, identifier or photograph you take has a cost to the person who gave it. Ethics is **taking responsibly**: keeping that cost proportionate to the benefit and making sure the person bearing it agreed. Try listing the costs in your own next survey.
notes.5: Ethics runs from the research question to how findings are used. The left column of the table is the one to keep: judgements made continuously, in the field, tested when nobody checks. **An approved protocol cannot anticipate most real decisions**, so keep a written record of dilemmas and how you resolved them.
notes.6: Power is the reason ethics exists. The researcher brings institutional backing, control of the questions and the power to publish, and the participant often has no route to complain. The last row is the quiet one: **a link to a benefit makes refusal feel costly**. Say participation is unconnected to benefits, and make that true.
notes.7: Participants should shape what is asked, see what was found, withdraw, and keep a stake. The test is simple: could you explain the study candidly and in full to the people in it, and would they still agree? A light version helps: **show the questionnaire to a few community members before fielding it**.
notes.8: Four ordinary causes of ethical failure: convenience, pressure, distance and habit, with optimism as a fifth in the table. None needs bad intent. The structural counter is to **give someone in the team explicit responsibility for raising the ethical question**, so it is not everyone's job and therefore nobody's.
notes.9: Failure damages people, truth, trust and your organisation. The row to quote to sceptics is truth: coerced answers are unreliable answers, so **ethics and data quality rise together**. A participant who cannot refuse also cannot say 'I do not know', and the dataset fills with confident, invented answers.
notes.10: The roadmap splits the course into foundations and practice. Foundations cover why ethics matters, history, the three principles and consent. Practice covers vulnerable groups, privacy, harm, review in India, field dilemmas, data ethics and checklists. Examples come from India and the region, which are **the conditions you will actually work in**.
notes.12: Each code answers a documented abuse: Nuremberg experiments on prisoners, Helsinki continuing medical abuses, Belmont Tuskegee, CIOMS research in poor countries. Because codes followed exposures, they read as specific prohibitions. **They also lag current practice**: data-driven research raised questions none of them anticipated, which section 10 addresses.
notes.13: The Nuremberg Code of 1947 is the first international statement that research on humans requires consent. Remember its four commitments: voluntary consent is absolutely essential, participants may withdraw, risks must be justified, avoidable suffering must be prevented. Its absolutism had a limit: **it made no provision for people who cannot consent**.
notes.14: Helsinki turned principles into working guidance for medical research. Its most consequential addition for practitioners is that **the participant's wellbeing takes priority over science and society**. The 1975 revision introduced independent ethics review. Revisions track controversies such as placebo controls and publication of negative results.
notes.15: Tuskegee ran from 1932 to 1972: poor Black men with syphilis were observed and deliberately left untreated, even after penicillin became standard. Match it to the principles: no consent breaks respect for persons, the withheld cure breaks beneficence, and the targeting breaks justice. **It ended because a journalist published it.**
notes.16: Read the right-hand column of the table as a warning about your own work. The men were chosen because they were poor and powerless, which is the population development research works with. Note the second row: **a control group denied a benefit already known to work is not an ethical comparison**.
notes.17: Belmont gave research ethics three principles, each paired with a procedure: respect for persons with informed consent, beneficence with risk-benefit assessment, and justice with fair selection. The pairing made review operable, and it is also the limit. **A study can complete all three procedures and still be exploitative.**
notes.18: Use the timeline as a spine for dates: 1947, 1964, 1972, 1979, then CIOMS, 2017 and 2023. The lesson on the slide is uncomfortable: the 1972 entry is a newspaper story that produced more change than any code listed, since **the profession has generally reformed after exposure and not after reflection**.
notes.19: Early codes came from Europe and North America and assume written consent, individual autonomy, a cost-free refusal and a reachable regulator. South Asian reality differs on each count. The slide's closing point is the practical one: **none of this weakens the principles**; implementing them takes more work.
notes.21: Belmont's three principles each force a question: did they freely choose, have we minimised harm and is there benefit, and who bears the burden and who gains? They conflict routinely, so applying them means weighing and not checking off. **Learn them and you can reason through situations no checklist anticipated.**
notes.22: Respect for persons has two halves: honour the choices of those who can decide, and protect those with reduced autonomy. The second half is often read as permission to decide for people, but it means **extra safeguards and no exclusion**. Reduced autonomy is also situational: refusal is harder with officials present.
notes.23: Beneficence is an active duty to do good, and non-maleficence is the duty to prevent injury of five kinds. A study that harms nobody and benefits nobody has not satisfied beneficence. The slide flags the weakest point: **do the benefits reach the people bearing the risk?** Usually the knowledge benefits others.
notes.24: Justice asks who carries the cost and who collects the benefit. Look at the four failures: convenient populations, benefits flowing elsewhere, burden without feedback and exclusion from useful research. The last one matters: **excluding a group from research that would benefit them is also an injustice**, which is why safeguards are the answer to vulnerability.
notes.25: The same communities (Dalit, Adivasi, slum, migrant) are surveyed repeatedly while the powerful are rarely subjects. The right-hand column of the table is where much of the interesting evidence sits and it is under-collected. Before adding another survey of a well-studied group, **check whether the question has already been answered**.
notes.26: Ordinary fieldwork pits principles against each other: a survivor's disclosure, a woman who cannot be interviewed privately, a gatekeeper who selects participants, a finding that might stigmatise. The skill is **recognising the conflict and naming it aloud in the team**, because the default resolution favours whichever principle the deadline serves.
notes.27: Four newer principles come from community-based research: respect for communities, reciprocity, transparency and cultural humility. Each corrects an assumption in Belmont. The strongest case in South Asia is group harm: **a finding attached to a caste, a village or a religion damages people who were never surveyed**.
notes.28: Use the five questions before fieldwork and again before publication, since publication is a separate ethical act. Pair each question with its failing answer, such as 'They all agreed' for free choice. The table's last question asks whether the work could harm a group, and **individual consent does not cover harm to a community**.
notes.30: Consent needs understanding, voluntariness, disclosure and the right to stop. A signed form documents a process and does not constitute one. **Test comprehension: ask the participant to say back what the study is about** and what happens to their answers. A thumbprint on an unexplained form is not consent.
notes.31: All three elements must hold: voluntary, informed, comprehended. Each has a typical field failure: officials present, a form read at speed in the wrong language, or words heard and never checked. The third is almost never verified. **A two-question comprehension check adds a minute per interview** and is the most effective improvement available.
notes.32: Learn the six disclosures, then look at what is commonly omitted: who funds the work, the real time involved, social and legal risks, onward data sharing and the right to stop. Funder disclosure matters because answers may change. **Consent given for one study does not extend to a repository.**
notes.33: Where reading is not assumed, read the form aloud in the participant's language, check comprehension by having them say it back, and use an impartial witness. The test of impartial is strict: **a witness who is the sarpanch or the husband is not independent** of the pressure being checked for. Record oral consent.
notes.34: Voluntariness is fragile under unequal power. Counter each pressure: interview without officials, state the separation from benefits, offer refusal actively twice, and confirm privately when a gatekeeper has instructed people. **A refusal rate near zero in a poor community is a warning about the process**, and not a sign of good rapport.
notes.35: Minors need two things: a parent's or guardian's informed consent and the child's own assent in age-appropriate language. A child who cannot legally consent can still decline, and the refusal should be respected even if the parent agrees. **Treat assent as a veto.**
notes.36: Match the situation to who consents and the extra safeguard: a guardian plus assent for a minor, a legal representative for cognitive impairment, deferral in acute crisis, and community gatekeepers plus individuals for group studies. The line to remember: **diminished capacity means more protection, never less**.
notes.37: Consent is a living relationship: it can be withdrawn at any time, long studies need re-consent, new uses of old data may need fresh consent, and silence is not agreement. **Build the deletion route when you build the database**, because a withdrawal right that cannot be honoured is only nominal.
notes.39: Vulnerability comes from a person's situation, such as dependence on a benefit, restricted ability to refuse, stigma or legal exposure. It does not come from being uneducated or poor as such. Seen as a property of people, it leads to **blanket exclusions**. Seen as a property of the situation, it leads to safeguards.
notes.40: Use the first table to map risk by group, and the second to match each group to a safeguard. Vulnerabilities stack, so a poor, Dalit, disabled woman needs the safeguards for all of them. Remember the last line: **your own design can create vulnerability**, as when a question about legal status makes an interview high-risk.
notes.41: For someone on the edge, a small payment can override free choice. Aim to compensate for time and cost, and never to pay for participation. Compare the amount with local wage rates and say what it is for. **An unexplained sum is read as payment**, and that creates the pressure.
notes.42: A woman's 'yes' may be her household's decision, and her answers on violence or autonomy could endanger her after you leave. Interview privately, use trained women interviewers and never disclose what she said. The final warning is sharp: **a researcher praising a candid response to her family has exposed it**.
notes.43: Findings on caste, manual scavenging or untouchability can brand a community and cause harm to people who never took part. Individual consent does not license that. Ask whether your framing could be used against the community, and **consider whether the group needs to be named at all**: the analytical point often survives without it.
notes.44: For refugees and undocumented migrants, the act of being recorded can be dangerous. The slide's rule is to collect the minimum identifying data, or none. Ask of each field what would happen if the file reached the wrong authority. **The safest data is the data you did not collect.**
notes.45: Survey fatigue is real and unequal: the same camps and bastis are visited endlessly with nothing in return. Costs show as declining cooperation and open cynicism. Respondents also learn which answers produce which responses, which is a data problem. **Before fielding, ask who else has surveyed here recently** and whether their data could answer your question.
notes.46: The answer to vulnerability is stronger safeguards. **Exclusion is no protection**, since leaving groups out designs programmes on evidence that does not include them. Use the five pairs: stronger consent, impartial witness, community consultation, referral routes and data minimisation. **Referral is the safeguard most often missing**: asking creates an obligation to know where to send someone.
notes.48: Keep the three ideas distinct. Privacy belongs to the participant, confidentiality is your duty and anonymity is a property of the data. You may promise confidentiality without anonymity, since you still know who said it. **Promise only what you can deliver**, and demonstrate anonymity instead of asserting it.
notes.49: Privacy is about boundaries, and violations happen in the room: arriving with officials, questioning before a crowd, probing beyond what was agreed, observing without saying so. A study can protect its data perfectly and still have intruded. **Ask where the person would prefer to talk** and let them decide.
notes.50: Confidentiality is kept in practice by storing names apart from responses, linking by code, giving need-to-know access, and avoiding informal discussion. The fourth row is where it most often breaks, since villages are small. **Brief field teams explicitly**; a signed protocol does not cover a remark between enumerators.
notes.51: Removing names is only the start. Village, age, caste, occupation and number of children together can single out one household, especially in a small area. Before release, **check the smallest cells**: a combination matching one or two records has to be coarsened or removed. Direct IDs go; quasi-identifiers need aggregation.
notes.52: Follow the four steps of re-identification: remove names, keep village, age, caste and job, shrink the area, and anonymity breaks without a single name. Each step looks reasonable alone. The standard remedies are **aggregating geography, banding age and suppressing rare categories**. All three cost some detail and prevent the failure.
notes.53: Risk rises sharply as the geographic unit shrinks. The same variables that are harmless in a national file can identify one family in a village. The rule on the slide is practical: **publish at the smallest unit your analysis needs and no smaller**, and coarsen aggressively for small places.
notes.54: Most breaches are mundane: a lost phone, an open spreadsheet, a forwarded email. The checklist covers encryption, unique passwords, a separate name-code key, deleting identifiers and securing paper. **Paper is the most-forgotten risk.** Set a deletion date at the start, since data kept 'in case' has no end date for its risk.
notes.55: Health, caste, religion, sexuality, immigration status, criminal involvement and experiences of violence carry higher stakes, and the harm of disclosure is severe and irreversible. Raise every safeguard and ask whether you need the detail at all. **Curiosity is not a justification for holding this risk.**
notes.56: Do not promise blanket secrecy, because a court order, a funder or a small sample can defeat it. Replace each over-promise with an accurate statement, such as 'We will protect this, and here are the limits'. Honest limits also improve data, since **participants calibrate what they disclose to what they believe about protection**.
notes.58: Social research is treated as low-risk by default, which is why its risks are under-assessed. Walk through the four assumptions: no needles, 'only a survey', 'we just observed' and 'nothing was published locally'. The Tuskegee row is the sharpest: **Tuskegee was observation**. Map every kind of harm before entering the field.
notes.59: Walk all five harm types through each study: physical, psychological, social, legal and economic. The table's third column shows timing: much harm occurs after you leave. So **harm assessment cannot rely on what the team observed**. A follow-up conversation weeks later on a small sample is the practical way to find out.
notes.60: The illustrative chart shows that the invisible harms, social, psychological and economic, dominate in development fieldwork. Physical harm is rarely visible because it occurs later. The slide's logic follows: **'we saw no problems' is not evidence**, and a short follow-up question weeks later is the only route to knowing.
notes.61: Read the matrix by likelihood and severity. High-high means redesign, and low-low can proceed. The cell handled worst is low likelihood and high severity, because rare catastrophic outcomes are discounted. For that cell, **prepare a response and keep the estimate honest**: know what you will do before it occurs.
notes.62: Minimal risk means no greater than daily life or routine interviews, but daily life differs by person. For an undocumented migrant or an abuse survivor, an ordinary question can carry far-from-minimal risk. **Judge risk through the participant's eyes**, applying the benchmark against their life and not yours.
notes.63: Follow the five steps: identify harms and benefits, estimate likelihood and severity, minimise by design, judge the residual risk and redesign or stop. Always ask who bears the risk and who gains. The slide's test of honesty: **the stop option must be available in practice**, or the assessment is decorative.
notes.64: Researchers and enumerators who hear accounts of violence, abuse and death can suffer secondary trauma. Distressed enumerators collect worse data and make worse judgements, so this is an ethical duty and a data-quality issue together. **Build debriefing into the schedule as a paid activity**, because optional and unpaid debriefing does not happen.
notes.65: Good design is the cheapest ethical safeguard: most harms are prevented at the protocol stage. Each mitigation has a cost, from losing a variable to needing time and logistics. Stating the cost makes the trade-off a decision. **Skipped questions are informative**, since the pattern of refusals shows which questions were unsafe.
notes.67: Researchers are poorly placed to judge their own ethics because they want the study to go ahead. Independence is the whole mechanism, so a committee drawn only from the running institution reproduces its incentives. Committees need lay and community members as well, because **a room of researchers shares assumptions that need challenge from outside**.
notes.68: The chart is illustrative, and the direction is real: ICMR's 2017 guidelines and clinical-trial reforms have made independent review the expected norm. The right-hand column is the catch. **Much social and development research still proceeds without formal review because nobody requires it**, and seeking it anyway marks a serious organisation.
notes.69: An IEC is India's counterpart to an IRB. Its composition requirements exist so the review is not a room of colleagues: independent members, a lay or community member, a legal member, gender balance and documented procedures. **Where your organisation has no committee, use an external or shared IEC.** Proceeding with no review is not an option.
notes.70: ICMR 2017 is India's principal framework, updating the 2006 version. Its reach is wider than clinical work: it covers social and behavioural research in health, committee composition, consent and vulnerable groups. Many practitioners do not realise much health, nutrition and wellbeing research falls within it. **Read the original and not a summary of it.**
notes.71: Four ICMR emphases: essentiality and voluntariness, non-exploitation, privacy and confidentiality, and accountability and transparency. Essentiality is the first and least applied: a study that duplicates existing evidence **imposes cost on participants for nothing**. Check whether the question is already answered before you design the instrument.
notes.72: Clinical trials of drugs and devices carry an extra regulatory layer under the DCGI and CDSCO, with registered committee oversight and defined compensation for injury. Most development research is not a trial, but the boundary matters. **If your study involves a drug, device or clinical procedure, check the regulatory position before designing it.**
notes.73: Know what an ethics committee asks: value and design, consent, risk-benefit, vulnerable groups, privacy and data, and justice. Notice that methodological soundness is an ethical question, since a weak study imposes burden for no benefit. **Submit consent materials in the local language**, as a committee cannot judge comprehension from an English form.
notes.74: Submit before any data collection and never retrospectively, include local-language forms, report changes and adverse events, and treat questions as help. **Retrospective approval is not approval**: data collected before review cannot be made ethical afterwards. Reporting an adverse event promptly is what a functioning system looks like.
notes.76: The protocol assumes a private interview, voluntary participation, neutral questions and a defined sample. The field gives a crowd, a sarpanch who selected people, a participant in tears and people wanting to be included. The protocol cannot foresee each case, but it can set **the rule you will apply** so you are not deciding alone.
notes.77: A gatekeeper's permission gives access, local legitimacy and a list of people, and does not give consent, freedom from their influence, a representative sample or voluntariness. **Every individual still consents separately, out of the gatekeeper's hearing.** A gatekeeper-selected sample also skews toward the compliant, so the problem is methodological too.
notes.78: Payment sharpens in the field: a crowd gathers when it is known, people answer to qualify and gatekeepers expect a share. Manage each: do not announce amounts publicly, screen before mentioning payment, pay participants directly and keep amounts modest. **Paying directly and privately after the interview avoids most of these effects.**
notes.79: Decide before fieldwork what triggers disclosure, to whom you would report, what you tell the participant first and who in the team decides. Warning someone after they disclose is a betrayal, so **state the limits in the consent process**. Know which reporting duties apply, including POCSO for offences against children.
notes.80: A photograph is identifiable data that travels into reports, websites and social media. Get separate consent for images, explain where they may appear, avoid framing that strips dignity, and default to no identifiable images of children. **Consent to an interview is not consent to a photograph**, and this failure appears in your own communications.
notes.81: Apply the family test to every image you publish: would I be comfortable if this were my family, captioned this way, seen by my neighbours and employer? The slide notes this is crude and works. Framing, caption and crop carry the same ethical weight as data collection, and **no committee reviews the annual report**.
notes.82: Emotional flatness, avoiding interviews, sleep changes and cynicism are signs of secondary traumatic stress, though supervisors often read them as attitude. Rotation, realistic quotas and a named person to talk to cost budget and protect both staff and data quality. **Caring for the field team is an ethics issue and a duty.**
notes.83: Use the five steps on any dilemma: name the conflict, identify who is affected and how badly, list realistic options, decide for the most vulnerable person's protection and document the reasoning. The fourth is the tie-breaker worth adopting: **where principles conflict irreducibly, protect the person with least power**.
notes.85: Ethics continues after the field through storage, analysis, ownership, sharing and reporting. These decisions come months after consent, usually by people who never met a participant and often without review. **Write the answers into the protocol before fieldwork**, so the decisions are made while participants are still in mind.
notes.86: Communities are surveyed repeatedly while knowledge, publications and value flow elsewhere. The table contrasts the usual answers with better ones: shared ownership, community use, benefit to both, and a copy left behind. **Leaving a usable copy of the data and findings costs almost nothing** and is the clearest practical reciprocity.
notes.87: Return findings in a form people can use, such as a meeting in their language, a poster, a radio spot or a conversation. A 60-page English PDF fails that test. **Dissemination back to participants needs a budget line and a date**, or it becomes the thing everyone intended and nobody did.
notes.88: Accountability runs downward to the researched as well as upward to funders. Name the funder, let participants challenge findings, report uncomfortable results and state limits. The third is the test of independence, since a finding suppressed because the funder disliked it is an integrity failure. **Agree publication rights before the work starts.**
notes.89: The DPDP Act sets duties for anyone handling personal digital data, NGOs and researchers included, from 13 May 2027. Size is not a ground for exemption. Section 17(2)(b) exempts research only when no decision specific to an individual is taken and the Second Schedule standards are followed. **Where Act and protocol differ, follow the stricter.**
notes.90: FAIR makes data findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable, and CARE asks about collective benefit, authority to control, responsibility and ethics. FAIR centres the data and CARE centres the people. **Open data is not automatically ethical data**, so hold both together, especially where a dataset describes a community that had no say.
notes.91: Open data advances science, yet releasing micro-data on marginalised people can enable re-identification, surveillance or stigma. Before release, check small cells, quasi-identifier combinations, whether consent covered sharing and who could misuse it. **Controlled access with a data-use agreement** is the usual middle path between open release and none.
notes.92: Honest reporting means no over-claiming, no cherry-picking, no writing that strips dignity and credit for communities and field staff. The slide's reminder: **the last harm a study can do is to misrepresent the people who trusted it with their lives**. Credit people by name where they consent to it.
notes.94: Answer the five planning questions in writing before fieldwork. The second row is the cheapest improvement: **if existing data answers your question, nobody has to be surveyed at all**. Also ask who bears the risk and who gains, whether a committee has reviewed the protocol and whether consent forms were tested in the local language.
notes.95: These fieldwork checks apply every day and not once at the start. Consent quality degrades as teams speed up under quota pressure. Watch for speed, a benefit implied, a crowd, blanket promises and missing referral routes. **Spot-check a few interviews yourself, unannounced**, since that is the only way to know what the consent process sounds like.
notes.96: After fieldwork, secure the data with the key kept separate, check the smallest cells before sharing, meet DPDP duties, return findings with a budget and a date, and delete identifiers on the date you set. The last row rarely happens because nothing forces it, so **put the deletion date in a calendar with an owner**.
notes.97: Treat the five sentences as alarms: 'they won't mind', 'no time for ethics review', 'the incentive is large', 'just remove the names' and 'we'll share results eventually'. The third is counter-intuitive: **universal agreement in a poor community is evidence about the inducement and says nothing about the study**. Stop and apply the principles.
notes.98: Keep six sources close: ICMR 2017, Helsinki, Belmont, CIOMS, the DPDP Act and your own IEC. Belmont is short enough to read in an hour. Before your next study, read at least the consent and vulnerable-populations sections of ICMR 2017. **They are specific, and they are what a committee will apply.**
notes.99: Five habits to adopt: treat every row as a person, treat consent as a process, add protection for vulnerability, check anonymity before sharing, and give findings back. Each can be adopted alone. **If you take one, take the second**: almost every consent failure in development research is a comprehension failure nobody checked for.
